claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a heterogeneous, naturally formed native oxide layer.
An anodic oxidation pretreatment can generate a controlled, uniform passive oxide film on Q235 steel.
The anodically formed passive film will suppress corrosion-related degradation in chloride-rich environments relative to the native oxide surface.
The passive film acts as a barrier to anodic dissolution.
The passive film impedes oxygen transport to the steel.
Reduced local anodic dissolution and oxygen transport suppress the initiation of localized corrosion.
An intact and stable passive film functions as an effective corrosion barrier under the specified exposure conditions.
Degradation of the passive film will cause corrosion rates to increase.
Pretreated Q235 steel will have lower corrosion current density than untreated Q235 steel.
Pretreated Q235 steel will have lower pit density than untreated Q235 steel.
Pretreated Q235 steel will have lower mass loss than untreated Q235 steel.
The untreated native oxide is less uniform than the anodically formed film.
XPS and EIS can quantify the relevant thickness, composition, uniformity, and integrity of the passive film during the study.
The hypothesis is scoped to aqueous 3.5 wt% NaCl exposure at room temperature and approximately 60 °C over designated immersion durations.

contradictions.description: The mechanism predicts that film degradation should lead to increased corrosion, whereas the falsification rule treats substantial film degradation itself as falsification. Film degradation accompanied by increased corrosion would be consistent with the stated conditional mechanism rather than decisively falsifying it.

The conditions describe passive-film characterization as in situ throughout temperature cycling, while the detailed design describes XPS as periodic surface analysis. The hypothesis does not clarify whether XPS is genuinely in situ or requires specimen removal and ex situ analysis.
